issues.issue: The recital defines "Defendant" as the two Wells Fargo entities, but the caption of the same instrument names "BANK OF AMERICA CORP. et al." as defendants, leaving the scope of "Defendant" in the operative paragraphs open to argument. No other provision reconciles the caption with the recital's definition.

The appeal waiver is conditioned on the Judgment being "entered as submitted by the parties," a condition whose satisfaction (e.g., after any judicial alteration) is not defined anywhere. That condition also interacts with Paragraph 14's Effective Date test, which turns on whether any party has "a right to appeal."

"[T]hose facts deemed necessary to the jurisdiction of this Court" is an undefined carve-out from the non-admission, and which facts fall inside it is not stated. Deemed by whom, and measured against what, is left open.

Paragraph 1's jurisdictional grant sits alongside Paragraph 13 (jurisdiction retained "for the duration of this Consent Judgment") and Paragraph 15 (jurisdiction retained six months past the Term for violations in the final Monitor Report), so the outer limit of the Court's power is set in three places. That is a possible but not obvious inconsistency.

Paragraph 2 makes compliance owed "in accordance with their terms and Section A of Exhibit E," while Paragraph 6 says the same Servicing Standards "shall be enforced in accordance with the authorities provided in the Enforcement Terms" of Exhibit E as a whole. Whether Section A alone qualifies the substantive duty, or the whole of Exhibit E governs, is a live enforcement question.

The antecedent of "which sum shall be known as the 'Direct Payment Settlement Amount'" is ambiguous: it may mean Defendant's own payment or the pooled fund including other institutions' money. That matters because Paragraphs 9 and 10 make the releases effective "upon payment of the Direct Payment Settlement Amount by Defendant."

Eligibility turns partly on borrowers who "otherwise meet criteria set forth by the State members of the Monitoring Committee," an open delegation with no stated standard or limit. The provision gives a court no benchmark against which to test criteria later adopted.

The obligation is to "provide" fixed dollar amounts of relief while "credit towards such obligation" is fixed only "as described in Exhibit D," so whether dollars provided or credits earned discharge the duty is not settled on the face of the paragraph. "Relief to consumers who meet the eligibility criteria" is likewise wholly dependent on the exhibit.

Paragraph 5 speaks of consumer relief obligations, while Paragraph 12's withdrawal remedy is keyed to "Consumer Relief Payments (as that term is defined in Exhibit F)," a differently worded term; the two may not cover the same obligation. Nothing in the body defines the relationship.

Paragraph 6 incorporates the Servicing Standards and Consumer Relief Requirements "as the judgment of this Court" but channels enforcement to "the authorities provided in the Enforcement Terms" of Exhibit E, which may restrict who may enforce and on what notice. Whether ordinary judicial enforcement of a judgment survives that channeling is a construction question against Exhibit E and Paragraph 18.
